Quick answer: Topical anti-inflammatory gels and creams can be effective for joint pain, particularly in hands and knees. They deliver pain relief locally with fewer systemic side effects than oral medications. Use them regularly, 2-3 times daily, applying enough product as advised in the leaflet. Avoid use on broken skin, and consult a doctor if pain worsens or new symptoms appear.

Overview

Gels and creams deliver pain relief with fewer systemic side effects — especially for knees and hands.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Versus Arthritis consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis Editorial Team and reviewed by our Clinical Review Board against UK NICE guidance and peer-reviewed sources. We update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Many studies, including large randomised trials and systematic reviews, have looked at how well topical anti-inflammatory gels and creams work for joint pain. They generally show that these treatments can be effective for pain relief, particularly in smaller joints like those in the hands and knees. The beneficial effects are often seen within the first few weeks of consistent use.

Clinical guidelines from major UK bodies, which are based on a review of this evidence, recommend topical treatments as a good first option for localised joint pain, especially for people who might be sensitive to oral pain medications. The idea is to target the pain precisely where it hurts, reducing the overall body exposure to the medication.

While not usually as powerful as oral medications for widespread severe pain, for many people with mild to moderate joint discomfort, these topical pain relievers offer a valuable way to manage symptoms without the higher risk of internal side effects associated with pills.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Not using enough: A pea-sized amount isn't generally sufficient; check the leaflet for guidance on how much to apply for your joint size.
  • Applying too infrequently: For best results, many topical treatments need to be applied 2-3 times a day, not just once.
  • Washing it off too soon: Give the gel or cream time to soak in properly before covering the area or washing your hands.
  • Using on broken skin: Avoid applying to cuts, scrapes, or irritated skin, as this can cause discomfort and poor absorption.
  • Ignoring the instructions: Always read the patient leaflet carefully for specific advice on how to use your particular product safely and effectively.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While topical pain relievers can be very helpful, it's important to know when your symptoms warrant a professional medical opinion. If you experience any of the following, please book an appointment with your doctor, physiotherapist or rheumatology team.

  • Sudden, severe increase in pain that doesn't settle quickly.
  • New, significant swelling, redness, or warmth around a joint.
  • Difficulty moving a joint, or new weakness in a limb.
  • Pain that wakes you from sleep consistently or gets worse with rest.
  • Any signs of infection, such as fever, chills, or pus around a joint.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use these gels and creams long-term?

For most people, topical anti-inflammatory gels and creams can be used long-term as directed, especially for managing chronic joint pain. However, it's always best to discuss ongoing use with your doctor, particularly if you have other health conditions or are taking other medications.

Do topical pain relievers interact with other medications?

Because very little of the medication gets into your bloodstream when applied topically, interactions with other medications are much less common than with oral tablets. Still, if you're taking blood thinners or have kidney problems, it's wise to check with your doctor or pharmacist.

How quickly should I expect to feel better?

You might start to feel some pain relief within minutes or hours of application, but it can take a few days of regular use to experience the full benefit. If you don't notice any improvement after a week of consistent use, it's a good idea to speak to a healthcare professional.

Practical next steps for Topical NSAIDs: Often Overlooked, Often Effective

If you came here about Topical NSAIDs: Often Overlooked, Often Effective, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Quick questions about Topical NSAIDs Often Overlooked

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
